title: 'He Can Bat Anywhere': Kotak Explains Why KL Rahul Is Invaluable to India
excerpt: Ahead of the third ODI against New Zealand in Hamilton, India's assistant coach praised Rahul's ability to open in Tests, anchor the ODI middle order and finish innings — and his habit of never looking under pressure.
body:
• India's assistant coach Sitanshu Kotak has called KL Rahul invaluable to the side ahead of the third ODI against New Zealand at Seddon Park, Hamilton, on Tuesday, November 10.
  • Rahul opens in Test cricket, bats in the middle order in ODIs, and can be sent in with five overs left to finish an innings — Kotak said he plays according to the team's needs in every format.
  • Rahul's unbeaten 26 off 38 balls on a difficult Wellington surface helped India win the second ODI by four runs under the DLS method.
  • Kotak said he cannot remember many matches since he joined the staff in which Rahul got an opportunity to bat and did not contribute — and that the batter never looks under pressure.

On the eve of the third one-day international against New Zealand, India's assistant coach Sitanshu Kotak made the case for the most flexible player in the side: KL Rahul, a Test opener who bats in the middle order in ODIs and, when the situation demands it, finishes innings at the death.

"I think KL Rahul's biggest advantage is that he can open in red-ball cricket and bat in the middle order in white-ball cricket. Whenever required, he can also go with five overs left. His record there is also very good. So, he plays according to the team's needs."

— Sitanshu Kotak, India assistant coach

Kotak, speaking at Seddon Park in Hamilton, pointed to Rahul's record across positions — at number five, where his record is strong, and at number six, where it is equally good — and to a consistency he described as near-faultless. "Since I have joined, I cannot remember many matches in which he has got an opportunity to bat but has not contributed," Kotak said, according to PTI. "He has played some unbelievable innings, and he never looks under pressure."

The Wellington innings that made the point

The immediate evidence came in the second ODI at Wellington, where Rahul's unbeaten 26 off 38 balls, with two fours and two sixes, on what Kotak called a tricky surface helped India close out a four-run win under the DLS method. It was not a big score; it was the kind of innings — composed, situation-first — that Kotak was describing. He added that Rahul offers experience and temperament, the ability to rotate the strike, hit boundaries and, when required, clear the ropes.

Why he bats at five

Kotak also explained the thinking behind Rahul's ODI position, on days when Axar Patel has been promoted ahead of him: one reason is the left-right batting combination, and the other is Rahul's strength in finishing games. Keeping a proven finisher back, rather than spending him early, is a deliberate construction of India's middle order — and it only works because Rahul accepts any number he is given.

What it means for the third ODI

India go into Tuesday's match at Seddon Park with their middle order settled around that flexibility. Whatever the match situation in Hamilton — early wickets, a platform, or a chase tightening at the end — Kotak's comments leave little doubt about who the coaching staff expects to absorb it.
nri_angle: India's most position-flexible batter goes into the Hamilton ODI with the coaching staff's public backing — the series context diaspora fans in New Zealand are following this week.
